J.I. Packer
jay eye PAK-er
proper noun (figure)
James Innell Packer (1926-2020), English-Canadian Reformed Anglican theologian. James (from Hebrew Jacob); Packer, an English occupational surname. Usually styled "J.I. Packer."

📖 Biblical Definition

James Innell Packer (1926-2020) was the English-Canadian Reformed Anglican theologian whose Knowing God (1973) became one of the most beloved and widely-read works of 20th-century evangelical theology, and who labored across a long life to recover the Puritans and Reformed experiential religion for the modern church. Educated at Oxford, Packer was shaped by his discovery of the Puritans (especially John Owen on indwelling sin and the mortification of sin) and became a leading voice for Reformed, experiential, doctrinally-serious evangelicalism. His 1958 introduction to a reprint of Owen's Death of Death in the Death of Christ is a landmark essay recovering definite atonement for modern readers (the dictionary's definite-atonement entry notes it). Knowing God (1973), his most famous book, presents the doctrine of God not as cold abstraction but as the ground of a transforming personal knowledge of God — doctrine for the sake of communion. His Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God (1961) showed that divine sovereignty and human responsibility are not at odds in evangelism but are an "antinomy" the believer holds together without resolving away either truth. Packer taught for many years at Regent College in Vancouver and served as general editor of the English Standard Version. The dictionary registers points of discussion: Packer's signing of "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" (1994) drew sharp Reformed criticism for appearing to blur the gospel distinctives the Reformation recovered, and some questioned his later ecumenical engagements. These genuine concerns notwithstanding, Packer's enduring gift was to make weighty Reformed theology accessible and devotional — doctrine that leads to the knowledge of God and the worship of Him.

J.I. PACKER, proper noun. English-Canadian Reformed Anglican theologian (1926-2020).

Oxford-educated; shaped by the Puritans (especially John Owen on the mortification of sin).

Author of Knowing God (1973) and Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God (1961).

His 1958 introduction to Owen's Death of Death recovered definite atonement for modern readers.

Taught at Regent College, Vancouver; general editor of the English Standard Version. (Signed the contested "Evangelicals and Catholics Together," 1994.)

📖 Key Scripture

Jeremiah 9:23-24 — "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom... But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth."

John 17:3 — "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."

Philippians 3:8 — "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord."

Hosea 6:3 — "Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

J.I. Packer is corrupted when Knowing God is read as devotional comfort detached from its hard doctrine, when his ecumenical engagements are either ignored or used to dismiss his whole contribution, or when his recovery of the Puritans is forgotten behind his popular fame.

expand to see more

Devotional-detached-from-doctrine misreading. Knowing God is beloved as a warm devotional book, and some read it for comfort while skating over its theological backbone. Packer's whole point was that the warmth comes FROM the doctrine: one knows God truly only by knowing the truth about God — His sovereignty, holiness, wrath, grace, and majesty. The book is an exposition of the doctrine of God aimed at communion, not a substitute for doctrine. To read it as gentle inspiration detached from its hard theology is to miss Packer's thesis that there is no real knowing of God apart from sound doctrine of God.

ECT and the gospel distinctives. Packer's signing of "Evangelicals and Catholics Together" (1994) drew sharp and substantive criticism from Reformed leaders (including R.C. Sproul and others) who judged that the document blurred the very gospel distinctives — justification by faith alone — that the Reformation had recovered against Rome. The dictionary takes this concern seriously: the criticism was not pettiness but a defense of sola fide. At the same time, it would be unjust to let one contested document erase a lifetime of genuine service to Reformed truth. The mature course names the real concern about ECT plainly while continuing to receive, with discernment, Packer's enduring gifts to the church — Knowing God, the recovery of Owen, the defense of definite atonement, and his lifelong call to doctrine-for-communion.
